body.x: Most Shia couples meet their marja's rulings long before they meet each other — in the way their families pray, fast and give khums. But it is during a rishta search that taqlid stops being background and becomes practical. Is her father's permission required, or only recommended? Who may recite the sigha, and in what words? What exactly counts as a valid mahr? These are not questions a website, a matchmaker or this guide can settle for you. They belong to the scholar whose rulings you follow — and knowing when to ask, and how, is a skill worth having before the search gets serious.
What taqlid means in ordinary life

Taqlid is the practice of following a qualified mujtahid — a marja — in the rulings of Islamic law, rather than deriving them yourself from the sources. For most Twelver Shia Muslims it is simply how religious life is organised: you choose the scholar you consider most learned, and his published rulings — his risalah, or book of practical laws — become your reference for everything from prayer to business dealings. In the marriage search, taqlid matters because a nikah is a legal contract in Islamic law, not only a celebration. Its validity turns on details: consent, the spoken formula, the specification of mahr, the circumstances of the parties. Those details are exactly what a marja's risalah sets out. Two families can both be devout, both be Shia, and still plan slightly different ceremonies, because their marjas phrase some requirements differently — and neither family is doing anything wrong.
The questions that actually arise during a search

In practice, the marja's rulings surface at predictable moments. The first is the wali question: whether a bride who has not been married before needs her father's or paternal grandfather's permission, and how that changes with her circumstances. The second is the sigha itself — the Arabic formula of offer and acceptance — including who may recite it, whether the couple may recite it themselves or should appoint representatives, and how exact the wording must be. The third is mahr: what may be named as mahr, and how its prompt and deferred portions are treated. The fourth appears when a previous marriage is involved: iddah, the waiting period, carries precise rules about when a new contract may be concluded, and no couple should guess at them. A short list covers most of what families end up asking:

Does our situation require the wali's permission, and whose permission counts?
May we recite the sigha ourselves, or should we appoint wakils to recite it for us?
Is the mahr we have planned valid as we have worded it?
Has the iddah from a previous marriage fully ended?
Does anything in our planned contract conflict with the rulings we follow?

One more boundary is worth knowing. A marja cannot register your marriage with the state, and scholars' offices will generally tell you plainly that the civil registration of the country you live in is a separate duty — one you should not neglect, because it protects both spouses in law.
When the two of you follow different marjas

In the diaspora this is now ordinary: she follows one marja, he follows another, and both families are sincere about it. The working principle scholars themselves give is simple — each person remains responsible for following their own marja. Neither spouse is asked to abandon their taqlid at the door of marriage, and marriage does not merge two people's religious obligations into one. Where the rulings overlap, which is most of the time, nothing needs deciding. Where they differ on a point that touches the contract itself — the wali's permission is the classic example — the careful route is to satisfy the stricter requirement where that is honestly possible, or to put the exact situation to a scholar before the aqd, not after it.

Treat this as a conversation to have early, in the same spirit as talking about where you will live. Asking 'whose marja do you follow?' is not a test of piety and should never be used as one; families follow different scholars for reasons of teachers, language, region and trust, all of them respectable. What matters is that both sides know, well before the ceremony is planned, whether any ruling either family follows will shape the day — so the aqd can be arranged in a way both families can stand behind with a clear conscience.
How to actually ask a question

Getting an answer is easier than many people assume. Most marjas maintain offices and representatives — wakils — in the major Shia centres, and their official websites accept written questions, known as istifta, in several languages including English and Urdu. A good question is short and concrete: the facts that matter, and nothing that does not. 'A woman of thirty, never married, whose father has passed away and whose paternal grandfather is alive…' will draw a usable answer; a long story with names and grievances will not draw a better one. The resident aalim at your own centre can answer routine questions on the spot and will refer you upward when a question is genuinely unusual. Keep the answer you receive — the email itself, or a note of the ruling — with your marriage documents. If the question ever resurfaces years later, you will have the ruling as it was given to you, not a memory of it.
What scholars cannot decide for you

A marja rules on validity, not on wisdom. He can tell you whether a contract is sound; he cannot tell you whether this is the right person, whether the families will get along, or whether the timing is wise. Istikhara, family counsel and your own patient observation carry that weight. The healthiest searches use each resource for what it actually is: the community for introductions, the family for character, your own judgement for compatibility — and your marja, promptly and without embarrassment, for the rulings on which the marriage itself will stand.

excerpt: What taqlid means for the practical questions of a nikah — wali permission, the sigha, mahr and iddah — what happens when two families follow different marjas, and how to actually get a question answered.
title: The marja in Shia marriage: why scholars matter in the spouse search
